name: Release npm packages
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      dry_run:
        description: "Build and package everything, but skip npm publish"
        type: boolean
        default: true

# UNTESTED SCAFFOLDING — this workflow has never been run. Before relying on it:
#   1. Verify the aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu cross-compilation step actually links
#      (cross-compiling without a container is the most likely failure point).
#   2. Confirm an NPM_TOKEN secret with publish rights for the @oxc-react-docgen
#      org exists in this repo's settings before flipping dry_run to false.
#   3. Run once with dry_run: true and inspect the uploaded artifacts/tarballs
#      before ever running with dry_run: false.
#
# Builds and publishes two independent package trees from the same 5-platform matrix:
#   - @oxc-react-docgen/napi(-<platform>)   — native addon for the NAPI bindings
#   - @oxc-react-docgen/cli(-<platform>)    — the same crates/cli binary, wrapped for npx
# The CLI package is a thin process-spawn wrapper (packages/cli/bin/cli.js) — it contains
# no reimplementation of argument parsing, formatting, or serialization, so there's only
# ever one place CLI behavior can drift: crates/cli itself.

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always

jobs:
  build:
    name: Build ${{ matrix.target }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - target: aarch64-apple-darwin
            os: macos-14
            cli_platform: darwin-arm64
          - target: x86_64-apple-darwin
            os: macos-13
            cli_platform: darwin-x64
          - target: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
            os: ubuntu-latest
            cli_platform: linux-x64-gnu
          - target: aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
            os: ubuntu-latest
            cross: true
            cli_platform: linux-arm64-gnu
          - target: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
            os: windows-latest
            cli_platform: win32-x64-msvc
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.96.0
        with:
          targets: ${{ matrix.target }}

      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          key: ${{ matrix.target }}

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with:
          version: "10"
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "26"
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      # aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu needs a cross-linker — bare cargo build with the
      # target added is not sufficient on an x86_64 ubuntu-latest runner.
      - name: Install cross-linker (aarch64-linux-gnu)
        if: matrix.cross
        run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu

      - name: Build NAPI addon
        working-directory: packages/napi
        env:
          CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_GNU_LINKER: ${{ matrix.cross && 'aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc' || '' }}
          CC_aarch64_unknown_linux_gnu: ${{ matrix.cross && 'aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc' || '' }}
        run: pnpm exec napi build --platform --release --target ${{ matrix.target }} --manifest-path ../../crates/binding/Cargo.toml --output-dir . --dts binding.d.ts

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: bindings-${{ matrix.target }}
          path: packages/napi/*.node
          if-no-files-found: error

      - name: Build CLI binary
        env:
          CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_GNU_LINKER: ${{ matrix.cross && 'aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc' || '' }}
          CC_aarch64_unknown_linux_gnu: ${{ matrix.cross && 'aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc' || '' }}
        run: cargo build --release --target ${{ matrix.target }} -p oxc-react-docgen

      - name: Stage CLI binary for upload (Unix)
        if: runner.os != 'Windows'
        run: cp target/${{ matrix.target }}/release/oxc-react-docgen cli-binary-${{ matrix.cli_platform }}

      - name: Stage CLI binary for upload (Windows)
        if: runner.os == 'Windows'
        run: cp target/${{ matrix.target }}/release/oxc-react-docgen.exe cli-binary-${{ matrix.cli_platform }}.exe

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: cli-binary-${{ matrix.cli_platform }}
          path: cli-binary-${{ matrix.cli_platform }}*
          if-no-files-found: error

  publish:
    name: Publish
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with:
          version: "10"
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "26"
          cache: pnpm
          registry-url: "https://registry.npmjs.org"
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      # ── NAPI addon ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: bindings-*
          path: packages/napi/artifacts
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Move NAPI artifacts into per-platform packages
        working-directory: packages/napi
        run: pnpm exec napi artifacts --output-dir artifacts --npm-dir npm

      - name: Build vite-plugin (depends on napi's index.d.ts)
        run: pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/vite-plugin build

      - name: Publish NAPI packages (dry run)
        if: inputs.dry_run
        working-directory: packages/napi
        run: pnpm exec napi prepublish --npm-dir npm --tag-style npm --dry-run

      - name: Publish NAPI packages
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        working-directory: packages/napi
        env:
          NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
        run: pnpm exec napi prepublish --npm-dir npm --tag-style npm

      # ── CLI binary ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: cli-binary-*
          path: packages/cli/artifacts
          merge-multiple: false

      - name: Move CLI binaries into per-platform packages
        run: |
          for dir in packages/cli/artifacts/cli-binary-*; do
            platform=$(basename "$dir" | sed 's/^cli-binary-//')
            src="$dir"/$(ls "$dir")
            dest="packages/cli/npm/$platform/$(ls "$dir")"
            cp "$src" "$dest"
            chmod +x "$dest" 2>/dev/null || true
          done

      - name: Publish CLI per-platform packages (dry run)
        if: inputs.dry_run
        run: |
          for dir in packages/cli/npm/*/; do
            (cd "$dir" && npm publish --access public --dry-run)
          done

      - name: Publish CLI per-platform packages
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        env:
          NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          for dir in packages/cli/npm/*/; do
            (cd "$dir" && npm publish --access public)
          done

      - name: Publish @oxc-react-docgen/cli (dry run)
        if: inputs.dry_run
        working-directory: packages/cli
        run: npm publish --access public --dry-run

      - name: Publish @oxc-react-docgen/cli
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        working-directory: packages/cli
        env:
          NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
        run: npm publish --access public

          CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_GNU_LINKER: ${{ matrix.cross && 'aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc' || '' }}
          CC_aarch64_unknown_linux_gnu: ${{ matrix.cross && 'aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc' || '' }}
        run: cargo build --release --target ${{ matrix.target }} -p oxc-react-docgen

      - name: Stage CLI binary for upload (Unix)
        if: runner.os != 'Windows'
        run: cp target/${{ matrix.target }}/release/oxc-react-docgen cli-binary-${{ matrix.cli_platform }}

      - name: Stage CLI binary for upload (Windows)
        if: runner.os == 'Windows'
        run: cp target/${{ matrix.target }}/release/oxc-react-docgen.exe cli-binary-${{ matrix.cli_platform }}.exe

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: cli-binary-${{ matrix.cli_platform }}
          path: cli-binary-${{ matrix.cli_platform }}*
          if-no-files-found: error

  publish:
    name: Publish
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with:
          version: "10"
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "26"
          cache: pnpm
          registry-url: "https://registry.npmjs.org"
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      # ── NAPI addon ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: bindings-*
          path: packages/napi/artifacts
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Move NAPI artifacts into per-platform packages
        working-directory: packages/napi
        run: pnpm exec napi artifacts --output-dir artifacts --npm-dir npm

      - name: Build vite-plugin (depends on napi's index.d.ts)
        run: pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/vite-plugin build

      - name: Publish NAPI packages (dry run)
        if: inputs.dry_run
        working-directory: packages/napi
        run: pnpm exec napi prepublish --npm-dir npm --tag-style npm --dry-run

      - name: Publish NAPI packages
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        working-directory: packages/napi
        env:
          NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
        run: pnpm exec napi prepublish --npm-dir npm --tag-style npm

      # ── CLI binary ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: cli-binary-*
          path: packages/cli/artifacts
          merge-multiple: false

      - name: Move CLI binaries into per-platform packages
        run: |
          for dir in packages/cli/artifacts/cli-binary-*; do
            platform=$(basename "$dir" | sed 's/^cli-binary-//')
            src="$dir"/$(ls "$dir")
            dest="packages/cli/npm/$platform/$(ls "$dir")"
            cp "$src" "$dest"
            chmod +x "$dest" 2>/dev/null || true
          done

      - name: Publish CLI per-platform packages (dry run)
        if: inputs.dry_run
        run: |
          for dir in packages/cli/npm/*/; do
            (cd "$dir" && npm publish --access public --dry-run)
          done

      - name: Publish CLI per-platform packages
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        env:
          NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          for dir in packages/cli/npm/*/; do
            (cd "$dir" && npm publish --access public)
          done

      - name: Publish @oxc-react-docgen/cli (dry run)
        if: inputs.dry_run
        working-directory: packages/cli
        run: npm publish --access public --dry-run

      - name: Publish @oxc-react-docgen/cli
        if: ${{ !inputs.dry_run }}
        working-directory: packages/cli
        env:
          NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
        run: npm publish --access public

1	# oxc-react-docgen
2	
3	React component prop extraction powered by [OXC](https://oxc.rs). Parses TypeScript natively in Rust — no TypeScript compiler program, no type-checking pass, no startup tax.
4	
5	> **Status:** Core extraction, NAPI bindings, Vite plugin, and CLI are complete. Config file loading is the next milestone.
6	
7	## Why
8	
9	`react-docgen-typescript` spins up a full TypeScript `Program` to extract props. On a mid-size design system this takes seconds — enough to noticeably delay Storybook startup and make HMR feel sluggish. OXC parses each file in parallel with no type-checking pass, so cold extraction on a 15-component fixture set (shadcn, MUI, Chakra, Mantine, React Aria, Radix) takes **32ms**.
10	
11	The CLI can emit an RDT-compatible shape via `--format rdt` (see [MIGRATING.md](MIGRATING.md)). The Vite plugin and NAPI binding currently expose this tool's own canonical format only — not a drop-in RDT replacement at that layer yet.
12	
13	## Install
14	
15	`@oxc-react-docgen/napi` and `@oxc-react-docgen/vite-plugin` are not yet published to npm — there are no per-platform prebuilt binaries to install today. Until a release ships:
16	
17	```bash
18	git clone https://github.com/castrog/oxc-react-codegen
19	cd oxc-react-codegen
20	pnpm install
21	pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/napi run build:napi   # builds the native addon for your platform
22	pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/vite-plugin build
23	```
24	
25	`pnpm run build:napi` (not a bare `cargo build`) matters: it invokes `napi build`, which places the compiled addon exactly where `packages/napi/index.js`'s generated loader expects it. This works as a monorepo-local dependency today; there are no published per-platform packages for it to fall back to yet. See [MIGRATING.md](MIGRATING.md) if you're moving off `react-docgen-typescript` and want to know exactly what's compatible today.
26	
27	## Vite plugin
28	
29	```ts
30	// vite.config.ts
31	import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
32	import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'
33	import { oxcReactDocgen } from '@oxc-react-docgen/vite-plugin'
34	
35	export default defineConfig({
36	  plugins: [
37	    react(),
38	    oxcReactDocgen({ srcDirs: ['src'] }),
39	  ],
40	})
41	```
42	
43	Metadata is available on the `virtual:oxc-react-docgen` module and pushed via HMR as components change:
44	
45	```ts
46	import docgen from 'virtual:oxc-react-docgen'
47	
48	docgen.components['Button'].props
49	// {
50	//   variant: {
51	//     type: { kind: 'literalUnion', members: ['default', 'destructive', 'outline'], hasDefault: true },
52	//     required: false,
53	//     defaultValue: { value: '"default"', computed: false },
54	//     description: '',
55	//   },
56	//   ...
57	// }
58	```
59	
60	## CLI
61	
62	```bash
63	# One-shot extraction
64	oxc-react-docgen extract --src src/ --out docgen.json
65	
66	# Inspect a single file
67	oxc-react-docgen inspect src/components/Button.tsx
68	
69	# Watch mode
70	oxc-react-docgen watch --src src/
71	
72	# Shell completions
73	oxc-react-docgen completions zsh > ~/.zsh/completions/_oxc-react-docgen
74	```
75	
76	## Output shape
77	
78	```json
79	{
80	  "components": {
81	    "Button": {
82	      "displayName": "Button",
83	      "filePath": "src/components/Button.tsx",
84	      "props": {
85	        "variant": {
86	          "type": { "kind": "literalUnion", "members": ["default", "destructive", "outline"], "hasDefault": true },
87	          "required": false,
88	          "defaultValue": { "value": "\"default\"", "computed": false },
89	          "description": "Visual style variant.",
90	          "tags": {}
91	        }
92	      },
93	      "inheritance": [
94	        { "typeName": "ButtonHTMLAttributes", "htmlElement": "button", "omitted": [], "totalProps": 147 }
95	      ],
96	      "notableInherited": {
97	        "onClick": { "type": { "kind": "eventHandler", "eventType": "MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>" }, ... },
98	        "disabled": { "type": { "kind": "boolean" }, ... }
99	      },
100	      "discriminantProp": null
101	    }
102	  },
103	  "diagnostics": [],
104	  "stats": { "filesParsed": 3, "durationMs": 12, "dtsCacheHits": 2, ... }
105	}
106	```
107	
108	## Supported patterns
109	
110	| Pattern | Example |
111	|---------|---------|
112	| Function components | `function Button(props: ButtonProps)` |
113	| Arrow components | `const Button = (props: ButtonProps) => ...` |
114	| `React.forwardRef` | `forwardRef<HTMLButtonElement, ButtonProps>(...)` |
115	| HOC-wrapped | `styled(Base)<ButtonProps>` |
116	| Interface inheritance | `interface ButtonProps extends HTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement>` |
117	| Intersection aliases | `type ButtonProps = BaseProps & { variant?: string }` |
118	| `Omit` / `Pick` | `type ButtonProps = Omit<InputProps, 'value'>` |
119	| `ComponentPropsWithoutRef` | `ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>` |
120	| `VariantProps` | `VariantProps<typeof buttonVariants>` (CVA / TV / PandaCSS) |

Clean tree, committed. Here's where things landed after the pivot:

**What changed from the original plan:** Your "don't duplicate code" pushback caught a real problem before it shipped — I'd started porting `crates/cli`'s argument parsing, formatting, and RDT/Storybook serialization into TypeScript, which would have created a second implementation with no shared source of truth. Checking react-docgen/RDT's own CLI conventions turned up nothing useful (neither ships one), but it prompted the right question: crates/cli is already the tested, validated behavior — the fix is to call it, not rewrite it.

**Final shape:** `@oxc-react-docgen/cli` is a ~60-line wrapper (`bin/cli.js`) that detects platform, finds the compiled `oxc-react-docgen` binary (dev-local `target/release` first, matching `packages/napi`'s existing pattern, else a per-platform optionalDependency), and `spawnSync`s it with inherited stdio and the real exit code. Zero CLI logic duplicated. Verified end-to-end against the actual binary — `--help`, the `--format rdt` enum serialization, the `--src` validation exit-2 path, and the stdout/stderr split all forward through untouched.

**Bonus finds while wiring this up:** the release workflow I wrote last turn still had the same three flag bugs I'd already fixed in `package.json` but forgot to carry over here (`--cargo-name`, missing `--dts`, `-t npm`) — fixed those too, and extended the workflow to build both package trees (napi + cli) from the same 5-platform matrix rather than duplicating it.

Still `workflow_dispatch`-only, still no CI run, still no publish — same safety boundary as before.

fix(validate): read PropType fields by name instead of array index

propTypeToString assumed a tagged-tuple encoding (pt[0]) but PropType
serializes as a tagged object (pt.members/pt.value/pt.element). This
made every union/array/tuple/literal prop resolve to undefined, and
crashed entirely on any component with a union-kind prop (react-aria,
shadcn) since .map() was called on the result. Also picks up the real
eventHandler paramName instead of a hardcoded "event" placeholder.
EOF
)"

Committed as `5a458fd`. Clean tree aside from the two pre-existing untracked plan docs.

## Validation summary

Ran `--format rdt` extraction across all 8 fixture libraries (67 components) plus the full `apps/validate` accuracy comparison against real `react-docgen-typescript`. Results:

- **No crashes, no errors, no warnings** on any fixture set.
- **Event-handler param names work correctly end-to-end**: `onOpenChange`/`onValueChange`/etc. now show real captured names (`open`, `value`) that exactly match RDT's own output for the same components — direct confirmation the session's fix is correct against real-world code, not just unit tests.
- Found and fixed a real bug in the comparison harness itself (`apps/validate/src/run-ours.ts`) — it read `PropType` fields via `pt[0]` array-indexing, but the actual JSON is a tagged object (`{kind, members/value/element}`). This silently produced garbage type strings for every union/array/tuple/literal prop and crashed outright on react-aria/shadcn. Not a regression from this session — last touched 2026-06-28, so pre-existing and simply never caught before.
- After the harness fix, coverage sits at 240/2079 props (12% of RDT's raw total), but every gap traces to something already documented in `MIGRATING.md`: the curated `notableInherited` set (~15-20 attrs) vs RDT's full HTML attribute expansion (~250-300), and the intentional `ref`/`key` omission. Where we do model props directly, matches are exact (Chip 2/2, Avatar 3/3) or short only by `ref`/`key` (Select 8/9, Accordion 5/7, IconButton 5/7).

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
The harness bug is a good example of why "0% coverage" numbers demand investigation before being trusted as a regression signal. `pt[0]` on a JS object (not an array) returns `undefined` — no TypeError, no warning, just silent wrong data for every stringLiteral/numberLiteral/boolLiteral prop, and a hard crash the moment `.map()` was called on that `undefined` for a union/array/tuple prop. Because `run-ours.ts` wraps each library's entire extraction in one try/catch, a crash on any single component (like MUI's `Button.color` union) blew away *all* already-computed results for that library, not just the offending component — which is why the failure mode looked like "found nothing" rather than "found something with wrong types."
─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

No further scope was pursued — the release workflow remains `workflow_dispatch`-only with no CI trigger and no publish, matching your explicit scope choices from earlier in this session.
Do we produce better results than RDT? That is one of our goals

1	# Migrating from react-docgen-typescript
2	
3	`oxc-react-docgen` targets output-shape compatibility with `react-docgen-typescript` (RDT) via the CLI's `--format rdt` flag. The NAPI binding and Vite plugin currently only expose the tool's own canonical format (`kind`-tagged `PropType`, shown in the main README) — there's no RDT-shape option at that layer yet. This document covers what's compatible today, what's intentionally different, and what's a known gap rather than a design choice.
4	
5	**Should you switch today?** If your components use plain interfaces/type aliases, `forwardRef`, `FC`, HOC wrapping, `Omit`/`Pick`, or `VariantProps` (CVA/TV/PandaCSS) — yes, output should match closely. If you scrape the full 250+ inherited HTML attributes per component, or rely on deeply nested discriminated unions, read the [HTML attribute inheritance](#html-attribute-inheritance) and [Known bugs](#known-bugs-not-design-choices) sections below first.
6	
7	## Field-by-field comparison
8	
9	### Component level (`ComponentDoc`)
10	
11	| RDT field | `--format rdt` | Notes |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| `displayName` | ✅ | |
14	| `description` | ✅ | From the component's own leading JSDoc, if any |
15	| `props` | ✅ | See prop-level table below |
16	| `methods` | ✅ (always `[]`) | RDT only populates this for class components; we don't support class components, so it's always empty — present for shape compatibility, not because we detect methods |
17	| `tags` | ✅ | JSDoc `@tag` values on the component declaration (e.g. `@deprecated`, `@since`) — not part of RDT's original spec but included since some tooling reads it |
18	
19	### Prop level (`PropItem`)
20	
21	| RDT field | `--format rdt` | Notes |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| `name` | ✅ | |
24	| `required` | ✅ | |
25	| `type.name` | ✅ | Literal unions emit `{name: "enum", value: [...]}` matching RDT's convention (so Storybook-style `<select>` controls activate) instead of inlining the literal text |
26	| `description` | ✅ | |
27	| `defaultValue` | ✅ | `{value, computed}` — captured from destructured parameter defaults (`{ variant = 'primary' }`) or JSDoc `@default`, code value wins on conflict |
28	| `parent.name` / `parent.fileName` | ✅ | `fileName` is always canonicalized to an absolute path regardless of how `--src` was invoked |
29	| `declarations` | ❌ not emitted in `--format rdt` | Only present in `--format canonical` (the raw internal shape); omitted from both `--format rdt` and `--format storybook` to match RDT's single-parent shape. File an issue if you need it |
30	
31	### Intentionally omitted
32	
33	| Prop | Why |
34	|---|---|
35	| `ref` | Not a user-facing prop — a React internal. RDT includes it because it walks the full inherited type; we treat it as noise |
36	| `key` | Same reasoning as `ref` |
37	
38	### HTML attribute inheritance
39	
40	RDT inlines every inherited HTML attribute (e.g. all ~250-300 members of `ButtonHTMLAttributes`) directly into `props`. We don't — instead:
41	
42	- `inheritance` (canonical format only) records the layer itself (`ButtonHTMLAttributes`, the element it maps to, what was `Omit`-ted).
43	- `notableInherited` surfaces ~15-20 curated, commonly-documented HTML attributes per element (`onClick`, `disabled`, `type`, ARIA attributes, etc.) rather than the full set.
44	- `--format rdt` does **not** include `notableInherited` at all — RDT consumers that filter by `parent.fileName.includes('node_modules')` to drop inherited noise will simply see fewer inherited props than RDT provides, not extra/wrong ones.
45	
46	If your tooling depends on the full inherited-attribute list being present, this is the biggest real compatibility gap — not a bug, but a deliberate scope decision to keep output focused on what a component actually documents.
47	
48	## Known bugs, not design choices
49	
50	These are tracked in [docs/rdt-coverage.md](docs/rdt-coverage.md) and get fixed over time — check that file for current status before assuming a mismatch is permanent:
51	
52	- Discriminated unions (e.g. `AccordionSingleProps | AccordionMultipleProps`) union each conflicting prop's type across all members that declare it — matches RDT's behavior for the fixtures tested so far, but hasn't been exercised against every union shape RDT handles.
53	- `Pick<T, K>` / `Omit<T, K>` resolution depends on `K` being a literal string-union at the reference site; a `K` that's itself an aliased type may not resolve.
54	
55	## Getting the exact diff for your codebase
56	
57	`apps/validate/` in this repo is the harness used to compare this tool's output against a real `react-docgen-typescript` run, field by field, across several real component libraries (shadcn, MUI, Chakra, Mantine, React Aria, Radix). Run `pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/validate compare:all` against your own components if you need a concrete list of diffs before switching, rather than trusting this document alone.
58

## Known bugs (discovered via fixtures)

### Bug: method-shorthand handler loses param type

**Fixture:** `fixtures/rdt-compat/controlled.tsx`

**Symptom:** `onValueChange?(value: string): void` (TSMethodSignature form) emits `eventType: "..."` instead of `eventType: "string"`.

**Comparison:** Arrow-function form `onOpenChange?: (open: boolean) => void` correctly emits `eventType: "boolean"`.

**Root cause:** The extractor's method-signature handling doesn't extract parameter types the same way as property-signature handling. TSMethodSignature parameters are stored differently from TSFunctionType parameters.

**Impact:** All real Radix UI `.d.ts` handler props use method-shorthand syntax. Every handler in Radix Select, Dialog, Accordion, etc., will show `eventType: "..."`.

---

### Bug: `Pick<T, Keys>` not resolved even for source types

**Fixture:** `fixtures/rdt-compat/pick-source.tsx`

**Symptom:** `interface IconButtonProps extends Pick<ButtonBaseProps, 'disabled' | 'type' | 'form'>` — the `disabled`, `type`, and `form` props from the Pick are completely absent from the output. Only own props `icon` and `label` appear.

**Expected:** `disabled`, `type`, `form` should appear with `parent: { name: "ButtonBaseProps" }`.

**Root cause:** `Pick` resolution in `alias.rs` likely reaches `resolve_base_as_chain` which tries to find the base interface, but the picked subset isn't materialized into the extractor's `interface_members` map. The resolution either fails silently or returns an empty chain.

**Impact:** Any component that uses `Pick<LocalInterface, Keys>` in an `extends` clause loses all picked props. This is common in design system component families that share a base prop interface.

---

### Bug: union-of-interfaces root props type silently skips component

**Fixture:** `fixtures/rdt-compat/discriminated-union.tsx`

**Symptom:** `Accordion` with props type `AccordionSingleProps | AccordionMultipleProps` is completely absent from the output. No diagnostic is emitted. `componentsSkipped` does not increment.

**Expected:** Either the props should be merged (with `discriminantProp: "type"` detected) OR a `Diagnostic` should be emitted explaining the limitation.

**Root cause:** The resolver's component detection path checks whether the resolved props type is a direct interface reference or intersection chain. A union at the root level falls outside this check and the component is silently dropped.

**Impact:** All Radix Accordion-like components (union type per discriminant value) are invisible. MUI `TextFieldProps` as `StandardTextFieldProps | FilledTextFieldProps | OutlinedTextFieldProps` works in the MUI fixture only because it's handled via a different resolution path (likely the DTS special case).

**Workaround:** At minimum, emit a `ComponentDiagnostic` with kind `UnresolvableProps` so the caller knows the component was seen but not extracted.

---

### Bug: component description set to last prop's JSDoc

**Fixture:** `fixtures/rdt-compat/controlled.tsx`, `fixtures/rdt-compat/pick-source.tsx`, `fixtures/rdt-compat/memo.tsx`

**Symptom:** When a component has no JSDoc comment of its own, `ComponentEntry.description` is set to the description of the last prop in the interface instead of being empty.

Examples from snapshots:
- `Select.description = "Whether the select is disabled."` (from the `disabled` prop)
- `IconButton.description = "Accessible label for screen readers."` (from the `label` prop)
- `Avatar.description = "Avatar diameter in pixels. @default 40"` (from the `size` prop)

**Expected:** `description` should be `""` when there is no component-level JSDoc.

**Root cause:** The extractor's `find_jsdoc` proximity scan finds the nearest preceding block comment. When there is no component JSDoc, it finds the last prop's JSDoc instead (within the 120-byte proximity threshold).

---

## Note: slot recipes — partial support

`defineSlotRecipe` (PandaCSS) and `tv({ slots })` (tailwind-variants) are in the recognized callee list and benefit from the 2026-06-28 arg-index fix. However, slot recipe variant values are objects (`{ root: "class", header: "class" }`) rather than plain strings. content.text:
Now I have a complete, evidence-based picture. Here's the honest answer.

## Short answer: yes, in specific measurable ways — but not universally, and one gap I found while checking this is worth fixing.

**Where we clearly win:**

1. **Speed — the core value prop, and it's real.** Live numbers from the harness just now: ~8-9ms per fixture set on our side vs ~110-150ms for the same fixture set through real `react-docgen-typescript` (which pays a TS-Program-instantiation cost per invocation). That's a 12-15x differential on tiny fixtures, and it compounds at Storybook scale since RDT's fixed cost doesn't parallelize per-file the way ours does.

2. **We preserve meaning where RDT's type-checker gives up.** MUI's `sx` prop: RDT's real TypeChecker evaluates the complex generic `SxProps<Theme>` and gives up, emitting bare `"any"`. We recognize the pattern and emit `"SxProps"` — a consumer can actually tell what that prop does; `"any"` tells them nothing.

3. **We expose data RDT structurally can't.** Component-level JSDoc tags (`@category`, `@see`, `@since`) aren't part of RDT's `ComponentDoc` shape at all — we added it because some tooling wants it.

4. **Previously-tracked bugs are now fixed.** `docs/rdt-coverage.md` documents 4 "known bugs" (method-shorthand handlers losing param types, `Pick<T,K>` not resolving, union-of-interfaces components vanishing silently, JSDoc description leaking from the wrong prop) — I just tested all 4 against the live binary and every one is fixed. That doc is stale and undersells where the tool actually is.

**Where RDT still wins — one is architectural, one is a real gap I just found:**

1. **Conditional type evaluation** (architectural, not fixable without giving up the speed advantage): a prop typed `T extends "a" ? "yes" : "no"` — RDT's real TypeChecker resolves it to the concrete `"yes" | "no"` union; we show the unevaluated source expression verbatim, since not running a type-checking pass is the entire reason we're fast. Honest permanent trade-off.

2. **`raw_string()` throws away structure it already has** (this one's just a gap, not a trade-off): I traced `PropType::Tuple` and `PropType::Object` in `crates/core/src/types/output.rs:239-241` and found they render as the literal strings `"tuple"` and `"object"` — even though the actual member/field data is fully captured elsewhere in the same struct. Confirmed against live `--format rdt` output: a `[number, number]` tuple prop shows `{"name": "tuple"}` instead of `[number, number]`, and `CSSProperties & { '--accent': string }` shows `{"name": "CSSProperties & object"}`. This is real data we're already extracting and just not surfacing in this one code path.

3. **HTML attribute breadth** — deliberate scope choice (documented), not a quality gap: RDT dumps all ~250-300 inherited DOM attributes; we curate ~15-20 via `notableInherited`.

Want me to fix the `raw_string()` Tuple/Object gap now, since it's a real, scoped, low-risk fix (two match arms, not an architecture change)? Or hold it for later — it's new work beyond what you asked me to validate.
We're adding support for TS 7 and tsgo to close the evaluation gap, right? Can we make the HTML attributes default but configurable??

Let me ground this in what's actually documented before responding — I don't have prior context confirming a TS7/tsgo plan, and I want to check the current HTML-attribute implementation before scoping a change.

content.text:
**Performance cost:** I don't have a real number without prototyping — but I can reason about where the cost would land. The project's DTS parse cache (`cache.rs`, mtime+size invalidation) means `@types/react`'s interfaces would only be parsed once per `@types/react` version, not per-extraction — so it's not a per-file tax, it's a one-time cold-start cost that gets cached like everything else. OXC parsing itself is fast even on large files, so I'd expect the *parsing* step to stay cheap. The real unknown is the *resolution* work — walking `ButtonHTMLAttributes<T> extends HTMLAttributes<T> extends AriaAttributes & DOMAttributes<T>` and materializing every member. That's not something I can size honestly without building a prototype and measuring it.

**The real danger isn't speed — it's correctness risk.** `DOMAttributes<T>`'s ~40 event handlers (`onCopy`, `onCut`, `onPaste`, etc.) use React's own generic `ClipboardEventHandler<T>`-style types, which the resolver already knows how to recognize — that part's probably clean. But fully expanding these interfaces means walking into React's own generic-heavy type hierarchy for the first time at this depth, and `docs/type-checker-integration.md` is explicit that generic-parameter substitution and multi-level generic propagation are exactly the gaps we've deferred pending Corsa. I can't rule out that resolving `HTMLAttributes`/`AriaAttributes` fully surfaces a handful of new structural edge cases we've never hit before, the same way the rdt-compat fixtures surfaced the Pick/discriminated-union/method-shorthand bugs. It's not guaranteed to be a clean win on the first pass.

Given that, my recommendation stays the hand-authored static table for now — same pattern already used for the curated list in `react_types.rs`, zero risk to the speed guarantee, ships without opening a new investigation. "Parse `@types/react` for real" is a legitimate phase-2 idea, but I'd want to scope it as its own small trial (e.g., just fully expand `ButtonHTMLAttributes` and see what breaks) before committing to it as the mechanism, rather than build it blind. # TypeScript Type Declaration Resolution for Packages Without Built-in Types

Based on the TypeScript documentation, here's how TypeScript resolves types for packages that lack their own type declarations:

## Resolution Process

When a package has no `"types"` or `"typings"` field and ships no `.d.ts` files, TypeScript follows this precedence order:

### 1. **node_modules Package Lookups**
TypeScript performs a [`node_modules` package lookup](#node_modules-package-lookups) with this structure:

> For each ancestor directory of the importing file, if a `node_modules` directory exists within it:
> 1. If a directory with the same name as the package exists within `node_modules`, attempt to resolve types from the package directory.
> 2. **If a directory with the same name as the package exists within `node_modules/@types`, attempt to resolve types from the `@types` package directory.**

### 2. **Precedence Order**

1. **Package's own types** (via `"types"`, `"typings"`, or `"main"` with [extension substitution](#file-extension-substitution))
2. **`@types` scoped packages** (`node_modules/@types/<package-name>`)
3. **No types** (resolution falls back to JavaScript files, resulting in `any`-typed imports)

## Key Details

### Extension Substitution
If `"main"` is present but no `"types"` field exists, TypeScript will attempt [extension substitution](#file-extension-substitution) on the `"main"` path:

```typescript
// If package.json has "main": "./dist/index.js"
// TypeScript will try, in order:
// 1. ./dist/index.ts
// 2. ./dist/index.tsx
// 3. ./dist/index.d.ts
// 4. ./dist/index.js (falls back to untyped)
```

### @types Resolution
The `@types` lookup is **automatic** and does not require configuration. The documentation notes:

> All `moduleResolution` modes (except `classic`) follow this pattern... do not search in `@types` directories [in the second pass].

This means `@types` packages are checked in the first pass through ancestor `node_modules` directories, before falling back to JavaScript implementations.

### typeRoots Configuration
While not explicitly detailed in the excerpt provided, the `typeRoots` compiler option can customize where TypeScript searches for type declarations, but the default behavior prioritizes:
1. Package-specific types
2. `@types` packages in standard `node_modules/@types`

Clean. Here's the answer, and it turned out to have a twist my first read of the source missed.

## Yes, and here's exactly how

**This is real, documented TypeScript behavior** — I confirmed it against the official TS module resolution docs. When a package has no `types`/`typings` field and ships no `.d.ts`, TypeScript's own resolution algorithm automatically checks `node_modules/@types/<package-name>` before giving up and treating the import as untyped. It's built into every `moduleResolution` mode except `classic`. **RDT doesn't implement this itself at all** — it wraps `ts.createProgram`, so it inherits this behavior for free from the real compiler.

For us, the picture is more interesting. We depend on `oxc_resolver` v11.21.0, and that crate ships a dedicated `resolve_dts()` function (`dts_resolver.rs`) that explicitly claims to replicate `ts.resolveModuleName` — including the `@types` fallback with correct scoped-package mangling (`@babel/core` → `@types/babel__core`). We don't currently call it anywhere; our code uses the plain bundler-style `.resolve()`, plus one hand-rolled special case in `resolver/react.rs` that just hardcodes resolving the literal string `"@types/react"` instead of `"react"`.

**I tested `resolve_dts()` empirically rather than trust the source reading, and it doesn't work for react specifically.** `resolve_dts(from_dir, "react")` returns react's own `index.js`, not `@types/react/index.d.ts`. Root cause, traced in the actual code: react's `package.json` has an `exports` field (`{".": {"react-server": ..., "default": "./index.js"}}`) with no `"types"` condition. `oxc_resolver`'s exports-resolution branch finds a match via the `"default"` condition, treats "found *something*" as sufficient, and returns immediately — which short-circuits the loop before it ever reaches the `@types` fallback code that sits right after in the same function. Real `tsc` handles this case correctly (millions of React+TS projects depend on exactly this fallback); this crate's reimplementation doesn't, at least for packages shaped like react.

**Practical takeaway:** we can't just switch to calling `resolve_dts()` and get automatic `@types/<name>` resolution for free — the one case that matters most (react itself) hits this gap. The fix is small either way: wrap `resolve_dts()` with a one-line check — if the result isn't actually a `.d.ts`/`.d.mts`/`.d.cts` file, manually retry against `@types/<mangled-name>` ourselves, same as the existing `resolve_react_types_file` special case, just generalized to any bare specifier instead of hardcoded to react. That's a much smaller lift than either building a full remap table or expecting the dependency to handle it — but it's a real, small piece of work, not zero.
Let's tackle it
This is a good, concrete, well-scoped piece to build now — generalizing the `@types` fallback so it's not hardcoded to react specifically, following proper TDD.

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.

**"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting"**

TDD IS pragmatic:
- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)
- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)
- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)
- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)

"Pragmatic" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.

**"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual"**

No. Tests-after answer "What does this do?" Tests-first answer "What should this do?"

Tests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.

Tests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).

30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals" | Tests-after = "what does this do?" Tests-first = "what should this do?" |
| "Already manually tested" | Ad-hoc ≠ systematic. No record, can't re-run. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Testing Anti-Patterns

When adding mocks or test utilities, read @testing-anti-patterns.md to avoid common pitfalls:
- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior
- Adding test-only methods to production classes
- Mocking without understanding dependencies

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

package with no "types" condition) showed it stops at the first exports
match — even a plain JS one — and never reaches its own fallback code.

resolve_package_types_file wraps resolve_dts with that missing fallback:
retry against @types/<mangled-name> whenever the primary result isn't
actually a declaration file. This generalizes what was react-specific to
any package name, needed for resolving real HTML-attribute interfaces
beyond just React's own types.
EOF
)"

content.text:
Committed as `ad033e1`. Clean tree aside from the two pre-existing untracked plan docs.

## Summary

Generalized the `@types` fallback so it's not hardcoded to react specifically. Following TDD:

- **RED**: wrote a test calling a not-yet-existing `resolve_package_types_file` against this repo's real `node_modules` — real `react` (exports-only, no types), real `@types/react` present.
- **GREEN**: implemented it as a thin wrapper around `resolve_dts()` — try primary resolution, and only if the result isn't actually a `.d.ts`/`.d.mts`/`.d.cts` file, retry against `@types/<mangled-name>`.
- **Extra edge-case coverage** caught something real along the way: my first "happy path" test picked `class-variance-authority` as a "resolves its own types cleanly" example, and it failed — not because my fix was wrong, but because `resolve_dts` has a *separate* quirk (prefers `import`/`require` conditions over `types` when a package's exports mix them in one object, which `@types/react` doesn't do but CVA does). Swapped the test to resolve `@types/react` directly, which cleanly isolates the primary path with no ambiguity.
- 103 unit tests + 8 snapshot tests pass, clippy clean, `cargo fmt` applied by the pre-commit hook (re-staged and recommitted, per the established pattern in this repo).

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
This is a good example of why "read the source and reason about it" isn't a substitute for actually running the code, twice over in this same fix: my first read of `resolve_dts()`'s source led me to expect it would work correctly once called with the bare package name, and testing proved that wrong (the exports-shortcut bug). Then my *test's own premise* — that CVA was a clean "no fallback needed" example — was also wrong, for a third, different reason. Three separate false assumptions in one small feature, each only caught by actually executing something and looking at the real output.
─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

This closes out the specifier-resolution prerequisite from the earlier investigation. Still open from that thread: the 3 small extractor bugs (missing `EventHandler` names, `readonly string[]` handling, the obscure form-actions type) and the actual "full HTML attribute expansion" mode wiring (CLI flag/NAPI option/config file, config.rs unstubbing). Let me know which piece you want next.
Can we run through the compiled source against and compare to RDT to check where we still have embarassing gaps? Can we look for some library or design system repos that we could validate against?
Not logged in · Please run /login

Two separate tracks here — let me run the gap-hunt on our existing fixtures directly (I already have the binary and harness set up), and in parallel dispatch a research agent to scout new design-system repos worth pulling in for broader coverage.

input.prompt:
I'm researching candidate open-source React component libraries / design systems to use as NEW validation fixtures for a tool called oxc-react-docgen (a fast Rust/OXC-based alternative to react-docgen-typescript, i.e. "RDT" — a tool that extracts React component prop documentation from TypeScript source by walking the type system).

Current fixture coverage (already in the repo at fixtures/, do NOT recommend these): shadcn/ui, Radix UI primitives, MUI (Material UI), Chakra UI, Mantine, React Aria (Adobe's react-aria-components), PandaCSS-based components.

I need recommendations for 4-6 ADDITIONAL real-world, actively-maintained, permissively-licensed (MIT/Apache-2.0 preferred) React + TypeScript component libraries or design systems that would make good NEW validation fixtures — specifically ones likely to stress different or harder TypeScript patterns than what's already covered, such as:
- Deep generic component patterns (polymorphic `as` props, `ComponentPropsWithRef<T>`)
- Compound/slot component patterns (Component.Root, Component.Trigger, etc. with shared context types)
- Discriminated unions for variant props
- Complex `Omit`/`Pick`/intersection type composition
- Non-trivial JSDoc usage for prop documentation (since JSDoc `@default`, `@deprecated` extraction is part of what's tested)
- CVA (class-variance-authority) or tailwind-variants based variant systems (different from what shadcn/panda already cover)

For EACH candidate, tell me:
1. Name, GitHub org/repo, license
2. Why its TypeScript patterns are interesting/different from the existing fixture set (mui/chakra/mantine/radix/react-aria/shadcn/panda)
3. Roughly how large/complex a single representative component (e.g. their Button or a compound component) is — is it something a person could reasonably read and manually cross-check output against, or is it deeply generic/hard to eyeball-verify?
4. Whether the package ships its own .d.ts types (self-contained) or requires DefinitelyTyped (@types/*) — self-contained is preferable since it's simpler to test
5. A concrete GitHub file path or two to a real component source file worth using as a fixture (verify the path actually exists via WebFetch, don't guess from memory — repos restructure over time)

Strong candidates to investigate (verify each, don't just assume): Ariakit, Headless UI (Tailwind Labs), HeroUI (formerly NextUI), Ant Design, Fluent UI React (Microsoft), Carbon Design System (IBM), Polaris (Shopify), Base UI (MUI's new headless library), Park UI, Arco Design (ByteDance), Geist (Vercel). Feel free to suggest others if you know of better fits. Use WebSearch/WebFetch to verify real current state (license, repo structure, file existence) — don't rely on training-data memory alone since repos restructure and rename over time.

Report back a ranked shortlist of your top 4-6 picks with the above details for each, under 700 words total. This is a research/recommendation task only — do not clone anything or write any code.

Confirmed still open. I have a complete picture now — writing it up while the repo-scouting agent finishes in the background.

## Finding #1 (the big one): most of our "gap" numbers were measuring against nothing

I traced why RDT showed `rdt=0` for every Chakra/Mantine/MUI/Radix/React Aria component in the comparison, and it's not a coverage gap — **`run-react-docgen-typescript.ts` explicitly filters out `.d.ts` fixtures** (`fixtures.ts:45` / `.filter(f => !f.isDts)`) because RDT's parser needs a real component (a function/expression that *uses* a props type), not a bare type-declaration file. Checking what's actually on disk:

- **chakra, mantine, mui, radix, react-aria — all `.d.ts`-only.** RDT never runs against them at all. Every "coverage %" and "ours-only" list I reported for these last time was just *our own output alone*, with no comparison happening.
- **Only shadcn (3 files), panda (1 file), and rdt-compat (9 files we wrote ourselves) get a genuine two-tool comparison.** That's a narrow, partly self-selected slice — `rdt-compat` was authored specifically to probe gaps we already knew about.

This isn't documented anywhere (checked `MIGRATING.md`, `docs/rdt-coverage.md`) — it's a real blind spot in how we've been validating. It directly explains *why* your instinct to find real library repos matters: we need actual `.tsx` component source from real design systems, not just their published `@types`-style `.d.ts` declarations, or RDT structurally can't participate in the comparison at all.

## Finding #2: within the fixtures that *do* get a real comparison, the results are clean

Went hunting specifically for embarrassing stuff — crashes, silently-dropped components, nonsense types — across all 8 libraries' canonical output:

- **Zero crashes, zero silently-dropped components**, zero cases of "RDT found real props, we found nothing" outside the documented HTML-curation gap.
- **Only one `Opaque` leak in the entire fixture set** — the already-documented conditional-type case (`string extends "a" ? "yes" : "no"`), correctly tagged with a reason.
- One diagnostic wording nit: `MantineColor` actually degrades to `Named { name: "MantineColor" }` (a reasonable, informative fallback), but the diagnostic message says "it will appear as opaque" — stale wording, not a real bug.

Of the type diffs against the real (shadcn/panda/rdt-compat) comparison set, most are non-issues once inspected:
- `(open: boolean) => void` vs RDT's `((open: boolean) => void)` — identical, just RDT parenthesizes union members.
- `"sm" | "md" | "lg"` vs RDT's `"enum"` — harness stringification difference, not a real type mismatch (we already emit RDT's own `{name: "enum", value: [...]}` shape correctly in `--format rdt`, confirmed in an earlier session).
- `sx: ours="SxProps"` vs `rdt="any"` — we're *better* here, already covered.

**One real, still-open gap confirmed**: `tokenStyle: ours="CSSProperties & { ... }"` vs RDT's fully-expanded `(CSSProperties & { '--accent': string; })` — this is the `PropType::Object`/`Tuple` `raw_string()` gap I flagged two turns ago (`output.rs:240-241` still hardcodes `"tuple"`/`"object"` literal placeholders even though the real field/element data is captured elsewhere in the same struct). Small, scoped, real.

I'll let you know as soon as the repo-scouting research comes back so we can decide which real component-source repos to pull in and close Finding #1.

**6. Still worth including for its `@heroui/styles` tailwind-variants layer intersected with the react-aria props, plus symbol-keyed context props (`[BUTTON_GROUP_CHILD]?: boolean`) for group-context propagation — a variant system genuinely distinct from CVA (shadcn) and Panda. `button.tsx` is small (72 lines) and easy to verify. Self-contained.
Files: `packages/react/src/components/button/button.tsx`, `packages/react/src/components/button-group/`

content.text:
All four fixtures are in and verified against real RDT. Here's the full picture.

## The headline number

On **unmodified, real-world code** from four separate design systems, our tool would have silently produced **zero components** for 4 of the 5 sampled components (Fluent Button, Base UI MenuRoot, Base UI MenuTrigger, and Ark UI's Select as originally authored) — not degraded output, just invisible. RDT correctly extracted all of them (303, 15, 293, and 314 props respectively). That's the honest "embarrassing gap" signal you were looking for, and it's real — none of our existing 8 fixtures exercised the patterns that triggered it.

## Root causes — 4 distinct bugs, but really 2 high-value fixes

| Bug | Hit in | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| **`forwardRef(...) as X` cast unwrapping** — none of our 3 forwardRef detectors unwrap a trailing `as` cast | Fluent UI (cast on the `forwardRef` call itself) **and** Ark UI (same pattern, independently) — 2 of 4 libraries, unrelated codebases | 🔴 Highest ROI — one fix, two real-world hits |
| **Same-file TS `namespace X { type Props }` resolution** — stored under bare name (`"Props"`), looked up under dotted name (`"X.Props"`) | Base UI — MenuRoot degrades to empty props w/ diagnostic; MenuTrigger is fully invisible with **zero diagnostics** (worse — silent, not even degraded) | 🔴 High — silent failure with no error trail |
| **`@deprecated` JSDoc bleeds onto unrelated sibling props** | Ant Design — `iconPosition`'s tag leaks onto `iconPlacement`, `shape`, `size`, `disabled` | 🟡 Medium — likely same root cause as the description-leak bug we already fixed once, recurring at prop level |
| **Generic type alias substitution** (`Assign<T,U>`-style user-defined generics) — `T`/`U` leak as literal unresolved names instead of substituting | Ark UI's original `SelectRootProps<T> = Assign<HTMLProps<'div'>, SelectRootBaseProps<T>>` | 🟠 Structurally bigger — worth its own scoped investigation before committing to an approach, same way the HTML-attributes spike turned out easier than feared |

One nuance worth flagging before you decide next steps: **the Fluent UI and Base UI fixtures currently sit "red"** (they still contain the real bug-triggering pattern verbatim and extract 0 components today) — good, honest regression tests once fixed. But **the Ant Design and Ark UI fixtures had to be rewritten away from the exact patterns that broke them** just to produce any comparable output at all, so as committed they no longer regression-test bugs #1 (Ark's forwardRef-cast) or #4 (Ark's generic substitution) — only bug #3 (AntD's JSDoc bleed) still reproduces in its fixture.

input.subject: Investigate + fix generic type alias substitution
input.description: Ark UI's SelectRootProps<T> = Assign<HTMLProps<'div'>, SelectRootBaseProps<T>> — resolver never substitutes type args into user-defined generic type aliases; T/U leak as literal unresolved names, props come back empty. docs/type-checker-integration.md flags "generic parameter substitution" as deferred/needing a real type checker, but that framing was about React's own builtin generics (DOMAttributes<T> etc.) where only the type NAME mattered. This is different: substituting concrete type args into a LOCAL/user-defined generic type alias body — may be tractable via structural substitution without a real checker. fix(extractor): qualify namespace member keys with their namespace name

Base UI's real pattern is `namespace MenuRoot { export type Props<Payload>
= ... }`, referenced elsewhere in the same file as `MenuRoot.Props`.
ts_type_name_str already produces the correct dotted name for that
reference, and the resolver looks it up as "{file}:MenuRoot.Props" — but
storage keyed only on the bare member name ("{file}:Props"), since nothing
tracked which namespace a declaration was nested in. Same-file namespace
member references could never resolve: MenuRoot degraded to an empty
component with a diagnostic, MenuTrigger (which references MenuRoot's
namespace from outside it) was fully invisible with zero diagnostics.

Fixed by tracking an enclosing-namespace stack during the AST walk and
having scoped_key prepend it. Confirmed against fixtures/base-ui:
MenuRoot 0 -> 15 props (exact match with real react-docgen-typescript),
MenuTrigger invisible -> 11 props.
EOF
)"

content.text:
Confirmed running cleanly overall (15 fixture libraries now, no crashes). Here's the complete round-2 picture.

## Round 2: 5 findings, 2 are real competitive gaps vs RDT

| # | Library | Finding | Vs RDT |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Blueprint Table** | Interface extending *two* different `Partial<X>` mixins silently drops the second one's fields (`defaultColumnWidth`, `maxColumnWidth`, `minColumnWidth`) — zero diagnostic, violates the project's own "never fail silently" rule | **We're behind**: 45 vs RDT's 48 props |
| 2 | **Day Picker** | Discriminant detection only fires when a type alias's RHS is *directly* a union (`type X = A\|B`) — when wrapped in an intersection (`Base & (A\|B\|C...)`, a very common real pattern), it falls into a naive first-branch-wins merge. `discriminantProp` comes back `null`, and `selected`'s type collapses to just `Date` instead of the real `Date \| Date[] \| DateRange` | **We're behind**: RDT gets the full union right, we don't |
| 3 | **Headless UI** | `forwardRefWithAs(NamedFn)`-style identifier indirection (the render function is a separately-declared top-level function, not inline) produces a *spurious, wrongly-named* component (`ButtonFn` instead of the real export `ListboxButton`) | Mixed — RDT gets the name right but explodes `PropsOf<TTag>` to 234–246 props from every possible HTML element and collapses `onChange` to `any` |
| 4 | Day Picker (secondary) | Bare function-type aliases (`type Handler<T> = (...) => void`) aren't classified at all, causing spurious "cannot resolve" warnings | Minor, unrelated to the union bug |
| 5 | Zendesk Garden | `styled.button.attrs<T>()` isn't recognized as a component-defining pattern at all | **Shared blind spot** — RDT misses this too (and produces a spurious false-positive elsewhere), so not a competitive gap |

Findings #1 and #2 are the strongest candidates — both are confirmed, well-isolated (Blueprint's agent already has a 10-line minimal repro), common real-world patterns, and genuine regressions relative to RDT rather than shared limitations. #3 is real but murkier (both tools have issues, just different ones) and #5 doesn't hurt us competitively.

input.subject: Fix Partial<X> mixin collision dropping fields silently
input.description: Blueprint's TableProps extends Props, Partial<RowHeights>, Partial<ColumnWidths> — only the first Partial<X> mixin's fields merge; the second (Partial<ColumnWidths>: defaultColumnWidth, maxColumnWidth, minColumnWidth) is silently dropped with zero diagnostic. Agent reproduced with a minimal 10-line case (two Partial<Interface> extends targets on one interface) — likely a visited-type/dedup key collision on the bare generic name "Partial" itself, ignoring type args. Confirmed regression vs RDT: 45 vs 48 props on fixtures/blueprint. TDD fix in resolver, likely chain.rs or wherever extends-list processing dedups by name.

result.output: Task #5 created successfully: Fix Partial<X> mixin collision dropping fields silently

input.subject: Fix discriminant detection for intersection-wrapped unions
input.description: Day Picker's DayPickerProps = PropsBase & (PropsSingle | PropsSingleRequired | ... 7-way union) — discriminant detection (find_discriminant_prop/resolve_union_alias in resolver/alias.rs) only fires when a type alias's RHS is directly a union (type X = A | B). When wrapped in an intersection (Base & (union)), the union falls into resolve_base_as_chain's naive CollectedType::Union arm which merges branches first-wins with zero discriminant detection. discriminantProp comes back null and selected's type collapses to just Date instead of the real Date | Date[] | DateRange. RDT gets this right. TDD fix in resolver/alias.rs.

result.output: Task #6 created successfully: Fix discriminant detection for intersection-wrapped unions

input.subject: Classify bare function-type aliases
input.description: type OnSelectHandler<T> = (...) => void style bare function-type aliases aren't classified at all by classify_type_alias in crates/core/src/extractor/alias.rs, causing spurious "cannot resolve" warnings on fixtures/day-picker. Add a case treating a bare TSFunctionType alias body as a Passthrough (or equivalent) to CollectedType representing the function type, matching how other passthrough alias bodies are handled.

result.output: Task #7 created successfully: Classify bare function-type aliases

input.subject: Fix forwardRefWithAs(NamedFn) identifier indirection naming
input.description: Headless UI's export pattern: function ButtonFn(props, ref) {...} declared standalone, then exported as `let ListboxButton = forwardRefWithAs(ButtonFn) as X`. Our extractor independently detects ButtonFn as its own spurious component (via the top-level PascalCase FunctionDeclaration path in visit.rs) instead of recognizing the real public name is ListboxButton from the variable assignment. Related to (but distinct from/worse than) the Ark UI forwardRef(SelectImpl)-style identifier-indirection gap already noted as a deferred follow-up during the generics investigation — that one made the component invisible; this one produces an actively wrong extra component. Needs investigation into same-file identifier-to-declaration resolution scope before deciding exact fix approach.

content.text: Confirmed the exact bug: `resolve_props_chain`'s cycle-detection key is `format!("{}:{}", consuming_file, type_name)` — using only the bare name `"Partial"`, not the type arguments. So `Partial<RowHeights>` and `Partial<ColumnWidths>` produce identical keys; the second call finds the key already inserted by the first, treats it as a cycle, and silently returns empty. Let me check how multiple extends targets merge, then write a TDD test.

fix(resolver): include type_args in cycle-detection visit key

resolve_props_chain's visited-set key was built from the bare type name
alone ("Partial"), not its type arguments. An interface extending two
different instantiations of the same generic — Blueprint's real
`TableProps extends Partial<RowHeights>, Partial<ColumnWidths>` — hit
this directly: both extends targets produced the identical key
"file:Partial", so the second one collided with the first's cycle-guard
entry and silently resolved to nothing, with zero diagnostic.

Fixed by folding type_args into the key. A genuine cycle (the same name
AND same args recurring) is still caught correctly; distinct
instantiations of the same generic no longer collide. Confirmed against
fixtures/blueprint: Table 45 -> 48 props, exact match with real
react-docgen-typescript.
EOF
)"

fix(resolver): detect discriminated unions wrapped in an intersection

Discriminant detection only ran when a type alias's RHS was directly a
union (type X = A | B). react-day-picker's real DayPickerProps is
PropsBase & (7-way union) — an intersection whose union member fell into
resolve_base_as_chain's naive per-member merge instead, which kept only
whichever branch's type happened to be seen first for each prop instead
of unioning across all branches. selected collapsed to bare Date instead
of Date | Date[] | DateRange; real react-docgen-typescript gets the full
union right.

Fixed by having resolve_base_as_chain's Union arm delegate to the same
resolve_union_alias logic a direct union alias already uses, and having
merge_parent propagate discriminant_prop (previously dropped silently
when merging a union's chain into an intersection's fresh one).

Also confirmed by testing against Day Picker's real interfaces: the union
is actually discriminated jointly on mode AND required (PropsSingle and
PropsSingleRequired both have mode: "single") — mode alone can't identify
the variant, so discriminant_prop correctly stays None there. That's
existing, correct behavior, not something this fix changes; the bug was
specifically the type collapsing, now fixed for both the simple and
double-discriminated cases.
EOF
)"

callee isn't React.forwardRef) nor try_hoc_wrapped (the argument is a

assignment, so the real export name never appeared at all: components
showed up as ButtonFn/ListboxFn/OptionFn instead of
ListboxButton/Listbox/ListboxOption.

similar after-the-fact rename: when a variable's initializer is (after
unwrapping any `as` cast) a call whose sole argument is a bare identifier
matching an already-collected component_mapping, rename that mapping to
the outer binding instead of leaving it under the inner name. Confirmed
against fixtures/headlessui: all three components now report their real
export names, matching real react-docgen-typescript.
EOF
)"

## Round 2 complete: 4 real bugs fixed, all confirmed against real code

```
0afb478 fix(extractor): rename identifier-wrapped components to their export name
2c3b109 fix(extractor): classify bare function-type aliases instead of dropping them
972f372 fix(resolver): detect discriminated unions wrapped in an intersection
249fa53 fix(resolver): include type_args in cycle-detection visit key
9254436 test(fixtures): add Zendesk Garden, Day Picker, Headless UI, Blueprint fixtures
```

| Fix | Real-world confirmation |
|---|---|
| `Partial<X>` cycle-key collision | Blueprint Table: 45 → **48/48** props, exact match with RDT |
| Discriminant detection through intersections | Day Picker: `selected` type now unions all 7 branches correctly; also discovered mid-fix that `discriminantProp: null` is *correct* here (mode+required jointly discriminate — not a bug) |
| Bare function-type aliases silently dropped | Day Picker: `OnSelectHandler<T>` no longer triggers a spurious "cannot resolve" warning |
| Identifier-wrapped components under the wrong name | Headless UI: `ListboxFn`/`ButtonFn`/`OptionFn` → correctly `Listbox`/`ListboxButton`/`ListboxOption`, matching RDT |

One of these (`discriminantProp`) needed real investigation, not just implementation — my first test passed with hand-built data that didn't match the real fixture's structure, which forced tracing into the actual repeated-literal-value shape (`PropsSingle`/`PropsSingleRequired` both declaring `mode: "single"`) before I could tell the fix from a false positive.

113 unit tests + 8 snapshot tests green throughout, clippy clean, every fix verified against the actual fixture that surfaced it before committing. Left out of scope per your earlier direction: Zendesk Garden's `styled.attrs<T>()` gap (shared blind spot with RDT, not a competitive regression).

The codebase now has 15 real-world fixture libraries total (11 from round 1 + 4 from round 2), all on a single working directory, no lingering worktrees.
What's next?

Given everything that's happened this session, here's what's genuinely left dangling, in rough priority order:

1. **Update `docs/rdt-coverage.md` and `MIGRATING.md`** — I just checked, and `rdt-coverage.md` still lists 4 bugs as "⚠️ BUG" that are actually fixed (verified live earlier this session), and neither doc mentions any of the 8 bugs found/fixed across the two validation rounds. This is stale enough to actively mislead someone reading it. Quick, low-risk, high-value.

2. **The HTML-attributes-configurable feature never got built.** We brainstormed it, investigated real `@types/react` parsing (found it's tractable and cheap), fixed the prerequisite (`@types` fallback), but the actual feature — curated-vs-full mode, CLI flag, NAPI option, and unstubbing `docgen.config.ts` — was never implemented. That's a real, scoped chunk of work still sitting open.

3. **The `PropType::Object`/`Tuple` `raw_string()` gap** I flagged early on (hardcoded `"object"`/`"tuple"` placeholders even though the real field/element data is already captured) — small, isolated, never fixed.

4. **A third validation round**, if you want to keep hunting — though we're likely hitting diminishing returns; the last two rounds found progressively narrower, more structural bugs, and a third round would mostly stress-test the same resolver machinery again.

My recommendation: **do #1 first** (cheap, prevents the docs actively lying to someone), then decide between #2 and #3 based on which you actually want next — #2 is the bigger, more valuable feature; #3 is a fast, isolated cleanup. I'd skip #4 for now unless you specifically want more coverage.

Prerequisite 3 small bugs found during the investigation spike but never fixed: (1) is_react_builtin in react_types.rs missing 4 *EventHandler names (ReactEventHandler, SubmitEventHandler, InputEventHandler, ToggleEventHandler) that @types/react defines identically to the ~19 already recognized, (2) readonly string[] not peeled correctly by TSTypeOperatorType handling in extractor/mod.rs (same category as the already-fixed Readonly<T> alias bug, just the array-keyword spelling), (3) an obscure indexed-access into React's DO_NOT_USE_OR_YOU_WILL_BE_FIRED_EXPERIMENTAL_FORM_ACTIONS internal (low value, can stay opaque). Also needs: PipelineOptions gains a mode field (there's already a dead skip_html_props: bool field in PipelineOptions/JsExtractOptions never wired up — natural seam), CLI flag, NAPI option (JsExtractOptions + binding.d.ts), and unstubbing crates/cli/src/config.rs's docgen.config.ts loading (currently hard-errors "not yet implemented" by design after validating the file parses as JSON) into a real JSON -> PipelineOptions mapping, confirmed in scope by the user during the original brainstorming.

fix(types): render real Tuple/Object contents in raw_string() instead of placeholders

PropType::Tuple and PropType::Object's raw_string() hardcoded literal
"tuple"/"object" strings even though the real member/field data is fully
captured in the same struct — real content thrown away in the one code
path meant to display it. Confirmed via --format rdt on the real
rdt-compat/types.tsx fixture: a [number, number] tuple showed
{"name": "tuple"}, and CSSProperties & { '--accent': string } showed
{"name": "CSSProperties & object"}.

Renders the actual TypeScript-like structure now: tuples as
[member, member], objects as { key: Type; key2?: Type2 }, quoting field
names that aren't valid bare identifiers (CSS custom properties, dashed
HTML attributes).
EOF
)"

fix(extractor): peel readonly/unique type operators transparently

readonly string[] (the type-operator form, not the Readonly<T> utility
type, which was already handled) captured its entire span as raw source
text unconditionally. Found while investigating whether fully resolving
@types/react's real HTMLAttributes chain was tractable: real
ButtonHTMLAttributes' defaultValue/value fields use exactly this shape.
Downstream heuristics reject a raw string containing a space, so it
degraded to Opaque even though the element type (string) is fully
knowable.

Peels readonly/unique the same way keyof already keeps its operand
structured, since docgen doesn't track mutability or symbol uniqueness —
nothing downstream needs the modifier preserved.
EOF
